73.0.0.en: 1- Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.

73.0.1.en: Imma: a conditional particle of emphasis, in his saying "imma" (truly).

73.0.2.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm declares and affirms that God is good, that is, there is no evil in Him. And this goodness of His appears to Israel, that is, His people who believe in Him and hold fast to His commandments. And Israel in the Old Testament is a symbol of the new Israel, that is, the Church.

73.0.3.en: 2- This goodness also appears to the pure in heart, who are able to see God by their purity, and love Him, and obey His commandments, so His goodness appears to them, and they accept from Him all His dealings, even trials for their purification. But the impure, that is, those far from God, do not see His goodness because of their rejection of God, although God is good to all.

73.1.0.en: 2- But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.

73.1.3.en: The writer of the Psalm confesses that he almost fell into sin, and slid down into it, and lost his spiritual balance. And this shows the following:

73.1.4.en: 1- His concern for repentance and confession, so much so that he confessed openly before everyone who reads the Psalm.

73.1.5.en: 2- His courage and his holding fast to the faith, for he saw that exposing Satan by declaring his sin enables him to resist sin by the power of God, and to reject the thoughts that almost made him fall into an evil deed. As for the heretics, they did not resist their thoughts, so they fell into heresies, and likewise the atheists.

73.1.6.en: 3- The necessity of being careful in all our steps lest we fall suddenly into one of the snares of the devil. It may begin with a slip, that is, a small fall, or a sudden great one, and it may be the beginning of sliding and sinking into a great sin, and a pit from which it is hard to rise.

73.2.0.en: 3- For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.

73.2.1.en: The writer of the Psalm makes clear that he fell into the sin of envy, and probably after this the sin of murmuring, when he saw that the wicked enjoy outward peace, and probably also success in their work and their lives, although he knows that God blesses His righteous children. And here he forgot that they have no inner peace; because sin creates disturbance in the soul. Many men of God have wondered at the success of the wicked, like the writer of this Psalm, and among them Job and Jeremiah (Job 21:7; Jer 12:1).

73.3.0.en: 4- For there are no pangs in their death, and their body is fat. 5- They are not in the toil of men, neither are they plagued like other men.

73.3.1.en: The writer of the Psalm adds that the wicked not only enjoy outward peace, but also:

73.3.2.en: 1- They are not exposed to hard afflictions at their death, and this may be the result of their riches, and their use of money to treat their illnesses and their problems.

73.3.3.en: 2- Their health is good, as he expresses this by saying that their bodies are fat, and not lean like the poor.

73.3.4.en: 3- They are not exposed to the troubles of poverty, sickness and ignorance, for they learn, and know what benefits them in their business, so their riches increase, and the trials that meet them are few.

73.4.0.en: 6- Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them as a garment. 7- Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish. 8- They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. 9- They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth.

73.4.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm shows the secret of the wickedness of the wicked, which is pride, which made them mock their righteous brothers, who may be poorer than they, or less healthy, and they spoke against them arrogantly, exalting themselves over them as if they had the authority of heaven, judging the people of earth, likening themselves to the angels and the inhabitants of heaven, although they are rejected by God because of their wickedness.

73.4.2.en: 2- As a result of the pride of the wicked they also fell into the sin of injustice, for they wronged those around them, whether by mockery and harsh words, or by coveting the possessions of others, because the wicked are selfish, and were not ashamed of their sins, but put them on like a garment, so they persisted in their wickedness.

73.4.3.en: 3- Since they were immersed in greed and lusts, the writer of the Psalm depicts their rush to eat and the desire of their bellies by the fullness and stuffing of their bodies until their eyes bulged outward. This affected their sight, and at the same time their insight grew weak, so they lost discernment because of their distance from God, and persisted in being occupied with material things beyond all imagination, for they became slaves of lusts.

73.5.0.en: 10- Therefore his people return hither: and waters of a full cup are wrung out to them.

73.5.1.en: When the people of God look at the success of the wicked, and come hither, that is, to this reality, which is this success, they grow weary and remain in the suffering of pains, and they drink them to the end, as a man drinks the waters of a full cup that fills his glass. And God allows this for the benefit of His children, and their approval, so they receive great blessings, and He helps them at the right time and supports them, and they overcome the thoughts of doubt and envy at the success of the wicked. This is as God allowed His people to drink the cup of captivity for long years until they repented and returned to God, and He gathered them and brought them back to their land, and they returned to worshiping Him in His Temple.

73.6.0.en: 11- And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?

73.6.1.en: 1- The wicked said that God knows nothing about what we do on earth, and this in turn made them regard sin as permitted, for no one will punish them; because God does not see them. This is the mistaken and foolish notion into which the wicked fell.

73.6.2.en: 2- There is another opinion on this verse, which is that when the righteous were exposed to sufferings, and their time and their suffering grew long, they said, Where is the God whom we sought? For He did not rescue us and restore to us our rights; so from the excess of their suffering they said that God does not know nor understand, for how can God's tenderness and fatherhood agree with our suffering and our pains? How can He neglect us and leave us? Yet God left them to suffer for a time for their benefit.

73.7.0.en: 12- Behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches.

73.7.1.en: The writer of the Psalm concludes this part by saying that the summary is the ease of the wicked in material respects, and their increase in gathering money by lawful and unlawful ways, so their success and their ease appear outwardly, although they suffer inwardly, and eternal torment awaits them, especially since they have been enslaved in their thinking, so their consciences no longer prick them, and they persist every day in their wickedness.

73.7.2.en: Remember always that God is before you and sees hidden things, and knows your thoughts and the feelings of your heart, and therefore do not accept evil lest you anger Him, and if you fall, rise quickly, and if an evil thought fights you, ask for His help, and then you will receive inner peace and enjoy true happiness in fellowship with God.

73.8.0.en: 13- Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. 14- For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning.

73.8.1.en: I have cleansed my heart: I purified it and made it good and clean. When the writer of the Psalm saw the success of the wicked and the pains of the righteous, he said to himself, I have labored much in purifying my heart and cleansing the works of my hands; because the result of it is sorrows, and on the contrary those who walked in evil have prospered, especially as he noticed that the pains do not end all the day, that is, all his life, since divine chastenings and daily sorrows meet him.

73.9.0.en: 15- If I say, I will speak thus; behold, I should offend against the generation of thy children.

73.9.1.en: The writer of the Psalm also felt that if he declared his murmuring and his doubt about the rightness of his conduct in righteousness and uprightness, he would stumble by this both himself and his sons if they were weak in faith. So that he would not make them stumble he kept silent, and kept his distress inside him, which increased his pains.

73.10.0.en: 16- When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me;

73.10.1.en: Finally the writer of the Psalm discovered that discussing all these thoughts mentioned above is wearying and futile, and consequently there is no need to continue in these thoughts. Thus human wisdom declares its inability to understand God's purposes, and man returns to God with prayer and praise so that He may give him rest and make him understand what he is able to accept from the hand of God.

73.11.0.en: 17- Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. 18- Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. 19- How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors. 20- As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image.

73.11.1.en: The sanctuary of God: the Temple of God, or heaven.

73.11.4.en: Terrors (dawahi): plural of dahiya, which is calamity.

73.11.5.en: 1- When the writer entered the sanctuary of God, that is, returned to God by prayer before the Ark of the Covenant, or in the Temple of Solomon, and asked for God's help, God made him attentive and guided him to see that the end of the wicked is destruction, because they walked the way of lusts, and slid down immersed in them, so they affected their lives, and brought upon them troubles and calamities and ruin, such as the lust for women, or wine, or any evil lusts that lead a man to many troubles while he is on earth. Indeed, calamities, such as diseases and problems, come upon the wicked suddenly, when they are unaware or on guard against them; because they are immersed in their lusts, so the terrors strike them.

73.11.6.en: 2- The sanctuary of God also means heaven, that is, when the writer of the Psalm reached heaven and learned of the glories of the Kingdom awaiting him, he rejoiced greatly, but he discovered that the conduct of the wicked led them to destruction and eternal torment. And death took hold of them suddenly, so while they were immersed in the lusts of the world they fell and died, and their riches or their strength did not benefit them. And it appeared clearly that the immersion of the wicked in lusts, and their dazzling life in all the material things they acquired, ended suddenly as if it were a dream, and they awoke from it and found themselves in Hades and destruction. Thus God mocked and despised the reliance of the wicked on lusts and material things, and they received the recompense of their evils, which is eternal destruction; for he who dreams of something great discovers when he awakes that it was merely a dream, and returns to his miserable reality. This is the end of the wicked.

73.11.7.en: Be faithful in holding fast to God's commandments and your upright principles, however much the wicked around you stray from the truth, and even mock you and try to draw you away from righteousness; do not let them, and persevere in your striving, for your crown in eternal glory awaits you.

73.12.s.en: (3) The salvation of those who rely on God

73.12.0.en: 21- Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. 22- So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee.

73.12.1.en: Was grieved (tamarmara): tasted bitterness and suffered greatly. I was pricked in my reins: I was pained as by a goad struck into my kidneys.

73.12.2.en: When the writer of the Psalm murmured against God, as appeared in the preceding verses of this Psalm, his heart was grieved like one who drank bitterness, and he was pained like one pricked in his reins, so he was in great pain, and therefore he decided in the end to keep away from all murmuring, and to rely completely on God, declaring his ignorance before the wisdom of God, and his complete submission to Him, and leaving Him to lead his life according to His divine will, as a beast is led behind the one who drives it, because the beast does not care about the hardships of the road or its straightness, for its leader is the one responsible; that is, man submits to God, and relies on Him, and leaves Him to arrange his life for him, and does not weary himself with thoughts of murmuring.

73.13.0.en: 23- Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. 24- Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.

73.13.1.en: 1- When the writer of the Psalm surrendered and relied on God, and rejected all the thoughts of doubt that attacked him because of the success of the wicked and the distress of the righteous, he enjoyed God's leadership, for He guided him to the right way by His counsel. And God's counsel is His commandments and His word in the Holy Bible, and indeed He held him by his right hand, that is, strengthened his works; because the hand symbolizes work, and He supported him with His divine power; because the right hand symbolizes strength. Thus the writer of the Psalm enjoyed fellowship with God, and experienced His great work in him.

73.13.2.en: 2- God brought the writer of the Psalm to great glory, by which he means the heavenly glory that awaits him after the striving of this life, or the rest he enjoyed after God brought him out of his trial, so he received the blessings of endurance.

73.13.3.en: 3- These two verses may be a prophecy about the affliction of the captivity, during which the people returned to God with repentance and faith, so God held them and led them to their land, and they enjoyed the building of the Temple, and the glory of worshiping God in His Temple.

73.14.0.en: 25- Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.

73.14.1.en: Since the writer of the Psalm experienced fellowship with God, and enjoyed Him, he felt that he needed nothing on earth except the Lord, and then in heaven he desires nothing but to see God and enjoy Him; for God has become his chief occupation, the delight of his heart, and his desires forever, and in this he declares his faith and his longings for the heavenly Kingdom.

73.15.0.en: 26- My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.

73.15.1.en: 1- The writer of the Psalm declares that if his flesh and heart fail, that is, he grows weak in body and soul under the pressure of the trials he passed through, he believes that his support is God his rock, and his portion, that is, that God is his refuge in whom he settles, and is his satisfaction who compensates him for all that he lost in the world, and therefore he does not fear trials, but they are his way to know God his rock and his portion, and in this he grows spiritually and enjoys fellowship with God.

73.15.2.en: 2- The writer of the Psalm also feels that in order to experience God and know Him, and for God to become his life and his portion, he must give up the material things of the world, and so become stripped and humble until he almost perishes, and then he knows God. And the beautiful thing is that he will enjoy God for ever, that is, he longs for a permanent existence in eternity.

73.16.0.en: 27- For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that go a whoring from thee.

73.16.1.en: The writer of the Psalm declares at its end that those far from God, that is, the wicked, however much they succeed in the world, or delight in the lusts of fornication and every evil lust, and reject God, which is spiritual fornication, nothing awaits them but annihilation and destruction in eternal torment, that is, they are deprived of all rest and of seeing God as a result of their evils.

73.17.0.en: 28- But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord God, that I may declare all thy works.

73.17.1.en: 1- And he decides in conclusion that he will draw near to God, keeping away from every sin, and that he is not disturbed by the success of the wicked, so he enjoys fellowship with God on earth, and then in heaven.

73.17.2.en: 2- The second decision is his feeling of the necessity of preaching to others who are far from God, so that they may believe in Him, and love Him, and live for Him, and not be drawn to evil. He does all this preaching while he is in the embrace of God his refuge, that is, living with God, so by His power he is able to preach to all those around him to keep away from sin and return to God.

73.17.3.en: When you see the success of the wicked, pray for them that they may awake from their heedlessness, and thank God who made known to you your way, so your holding fast to His commandments will increase, and you will even strengthen your brothers and establish their faith, so that they live with God always. A prayer that God not reject His people: a poem of Asaph, "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever?" (v. 1). Introduction:

73.17.4.en: 1- Its writer: a- Asaph, who is the leader of the singers, that is, all the choirs in the days of David (1 Chr 16:5).

73.17.5.en: b- David, and he gave it to Asaph to sing.

73.17.6.en: 2- When was it written? In the days of David, but it is a prophecy about:

73.17.7.en: a- The destruction and burning of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar in the days of the Babylonian captivity.

73.17.9.en: b- Or the days of King Antiochus (the Greek), when he destroyed and plundered the Temple in the time of the Maccabees (1 Macc 1:20-28).

73.17.10.en: c- Or the destruction of the Temple by Titus the Roman commander in the year 70 AD.

73.17.11.en: 3- This Psalm is suitable for every person who meets a great affliction, and during it may feel that God is late in intervening to solve the problem. And it is suitable for the whole Church when a great affliction meets her.

73.17.12.en: 4- There is a resemblance between this Psalm and Psalm 79, and both are by one writer, Asaph, as their titles mention. And they speak of the same subject, which is the affliction that befalls the children of God.

73.17.13.en: 5- This Psalm was written in the past tense to affirm the certainty of the occurrence of this prophecy, which was fulfilled literally when the enemy defiled the Temple by the entry of the Gentiles into the Temple of God, whether in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, or Antiochus, or the Romans.

73.17.14.en: 6- This Psalm is a symbol of Satan's destruction of man by making him fall into sin, but by the redemption of Christ He brought him back to life with Him.

73.17.15.en: 7- This Psalm is considered a lament for the Church, or the people of God, or the human soul, which is affected by God's separation from it; it does not doubt Him, but with sorrow it shows how weary it is at losing God.

73.17.16.en: 8- This Psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
